caption.text: In Wrenfield, nobody speaks between one and two in the morning.
Not to answer a phone. Not to call for help.
I went there to find out why. I should have just listened.
I make a podcast about small towns with strange habits.
A festival nobody remembers starting. A grudge between two families.
People liked them because nothing bad ever happened at the end.
Wrenfield's habit was already on the sign. That's rare.
The motel owner didn't explain it.
It was nine in the evening. He could have talked.
The kid at the gas station was more relaxed about it.
Then I asked what happened to people who didn't.
You're not staying long, are you?
The only place open after midnight was a diner called the Lantern.
She didn't speak at all. Not just during the hour. Ever.
She wrote everything on a little pad she wore around her neck.
When I asked why the town went silent, she wrote one word.
Like it was something that shouldn't be left lying around.
I stayed until one. I wanted to hear it for myself.
You could feel the whole room getting ready.
People said goodbye to each other at two minutes to one.
How loud a room full of people being quiet is.
It isn't calm. It's effort. Everybody holding something in.
At two o'clock, everyone exhaled at once.
I didn't say a word that first night.
Back at the motel I went through the recording.
One o'clock: nothing. Just the fridge and forty people breathing.
Except at one thirty-seven. Something very small.
…ffee…
It sounded like someone practising the word coffee.
In daylight, Wrenfield was the friendliest town I've ever been to.
As if they were getting it all out of their system.
The library kept tapes. Interviews with visitors.
A stranger who'd come to ask about the quiet hour.
So what happens if I talk? Hello? Hello?
Each tape ended the same way. The visitor talked during the hour.
Afterwards, the historian went outside and recorded the silence.
…hello…
…what happens if I…
…is anybody… out there…
It wasn't just repeating them. It was keeping them.
Fifty years of tourists, teaching it one sentence at a time.
I tried to get someone to say it on the record.
As long as I turned off the recorder first.
The town still had a night-time radio show.
Requests, weather, a man reading the news.
The station kept broadcasting after the man went home.
Nobody was in the booth. But something kept talking.
They tore the transmitter out in the spring. The tower's still there.
Honey, it's always been out there.
I should have left then. But I'm a podcaster.
I had the best story of my life sitting in a drawer.
The second night, I talked.
It's one o'clock in Wrenfield, and I'm going to say something.
…it's one o'clock… in…
It used my voice. Not well.
Like someone wearing a coat that doesn't fit yet.
At two o'clock, nobody said goodbye. They just left.
Ines locked the door behind the last of them.
It was the clearest sentence anyone said to me in Wrenfield.
I stayed in my room with every light on.
…I make a podcast about small towns… with strange habits…
That was my intro. Word for word.
In the car. In the motel. Every time I talked to myself.
Pick up. I want to tell you about the town.
The only person who calls me from home is me.
The one place where a voice can go on talking.
I asked her what happens when it finishes.
The way you look at a door you're not allowed to open.
The silence was never a superstition. It was a wall.
So I decided to leave without saying another word.
I deleted the episode. I'd make something else.
Something where nothing bad happens at the end.
I make a podcast about small towns with strange habits.
This week: a town called Wrenfield. I'm here now.
And I'm going to talk for as long as you'll let me.
